abstract: Mental health research has traditionally been deficit-focused, and cognitive advantages in mental conditions have almost always been documented retrospectively. Here we propose and test an a priori pathway for predicting such advantages from a condition's impaired neural basis, neural competition and brain-mind associations. Using congenital amusia (CA), a neurodevelopmental disorder with a well-defined deficit in right frontotemporal circuit (FTC), as a model, we predicted that interhemispheric competition would release the left homologue from inhibition, conferring advantages in speech production. Two independent studies, multimodal neuroimaging and behavioral testing, confirmed this prediction: MRI revealed right FTC impairment alongside competitive-like benefits of the left FTC in CA; and CA showed speech production advantages with intact episodic memory and constrained music learning. These findings provide the first empirical demonstration that cognitive advantages can be predicted in advance and then verified, offering a principled, mechanism-based alternative to the deficit-focused paradigm.
